Artificial Turf for Meadow Woods, Florida Yards

Meadow Woods is unincorporated Orange County land, about 7 miles from downtown Kissimmee, built out mostly between the late 1980s and the mid-2000s across many separate subdivisions rather than one planned community. The 2020 Census counted 43,790 residents here. A synthetic turf job answers to Orange County's permit desk, not a city hall, and to whichever homeowners association runs that particular street.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

An unincorporated community built one subdivision at a time

Meadow Woods has no city hall of its own. It's a census-designated place in unincorporated south Orange County, sitting between Hunters Creek and Lake Nona, just north of the Osceola County line, with Southchase to the west and Orlando International Airport to the east (Wikipedia's geography summary, sourced to the Census Bureau). Downtown Kissimmee is about 7 miles south. A homeowner typing "best artificial turf contractor near me in Meadow Woods" into a search bar is usually trying to sort out two separate questions at once: which office signs off on the work, and which HOA board wants a copy of the plan first, since this community grew as many small subdivisions rather than one planned development.

The 2020 Census counted 43,790 residents here, a figure that more than quadrupled the 2010 count of 25,558, which itself had more than doubled the 2000 count of 11,286 (Census Bureau QuickFacts; population history by decade). That growth curve is a rough map of when the housing stock went in: older, smaller lots near the community's core date to the late 1980s, and the largest share of homes followed during the 1990s and 2000s.

Two approvals, and neither one is automatic

Because Meadow Woods sits outside every city limit, Orange County's Permitting Services and Division of Building Safety reviews a synthetic turf project here, not a municipal building department. County Code Chapter 24 defines "turf, turf grass or sod" only as living grass species and has no section written for a manufactured surface (Chapter 24, Landscaping, Buffering and Open Space), which leaves the state's May 19, 2026 turf standard as the only rule written specifically for the material. The community's east edge, toward Lake Nona, sits close enough to Orlando's city limits that the boundary is worth checking before assuming which office applies: the county's own guidance is to read the street sign, since one marked "Orange" means unincorporated land, and to confirm on the Property Appraiser's parcel search (Orange County's annexation page). A parcel that comes back inside Orlando follows Orlando's own artificial-turf permit rule instead, which is a different process with its own engineering-permit step.

None of that settles the second approval. Fairway Townhomes at Meadow Woods went up in 1988 and 1989, Woodbridge at Meadow Woods followed in 1995 and 1996, and Wyndham Lakes Estates, on the community's east side, organized its own master association in 2005 covering ten subdivisions and 1,454 homes (Wyndham Lakes Estates; Woodbridge at Meadow Woods; Fairway Townhomes at Meadow Woods). Each of those runs its own architectural review, alongside smaller associations nearby such as Water's Edge, so a plan approved on one street says nothing about the next one over. We found no published guideline from any of these boards naming synthetic turf specifically, which leaves the state law limiting what an HOA can restrict as the operative rule: a board can't block turf that isn't visible from the frontage or a neighboring lot. Florida's 2025 turf law caps what a city or county can require and has nothing to do with what a board asks for on its own form; the HOA and ARC packet checklist covers what most of these boards want to see before signing off, whichever subdivision is asking.

Flatwoods soil, and two water districts meeting near Boggy Creek

Soils mapped across southern Orange County's flatwoods, the Immokalee and Basinger series among them, are sandy, nearly level and very poorly to poorly drained, built up in low flats and old drainageways rather than a well-drained ridge (USDA's Web Soil Survey; Immokalee series description; Basinger series description). That's a big part of why the two to four inches of washed, open-graded crushed rock or crushed concrete the state's turf standard requires is doing real work here: on flat, slow-draining sand, the base is what moves a fast summer storm off the yard, not gravity.

Meadow Woods also sits close to where two water management districts meet. The county's Upper Kissimmee Basin, which drains toward Boggy Creek along the community's north side and on to the Kissimmee chain of lakes, falls under the South Florida Water Management District, while most of the rest of Orange County answers to the St. Johns River Water Management District (SFWMD's Upper Kissimmee Basin plan; SJRWMD's district map). Retention ponds are common on the newer lots near that creek corridor, and the state rule keeps turf at least 10 feet from a pond, lake or canal edge unless a seawall already separates the two, with no exception for a drainage swale.

Water rules for whatever isn't turf

Orange County Utilities runs water and sewer through most of unincorporated Meadow Woods, on a seasonal schedule: two watering days a week during daylight saving time, one day a week the rest of the year, with no sprinklers running between 10 a.m. and 4 p.m. on any day (Orange County Utilities' watering restrictions page; the Water Division takes calls at 407-254-9850). None of that schedule reaches a synthetic turf area once the heads underneath are capped, something Florida Administrative Code — Rule 62-308.100, Synthetic Turf (effective May 19, 2026) has required statewide since May 19, 2026; it only governs whatever St. Augustine or Bahia stays around the new turf's edges.

Vacation-rental turf is a smaller share of the work here

Unlike the vacation-home pockets closer to Disney, Meadow Woods isn't zoned for short-term rentals as a matter of course. Whole-home rentals under 30 nights generally aren't a permitted use in unincorporated Orange County's residential zoning without a discretionary Special Use Permit, under an ordinance that predates the state's 2011 preemption on new local rental bans (a 2026 guide to Orange County's short-term rental rules). The county's vacation-home-friendly zoning sits in a handful of zip codes near Disney; Meadow Woods' own 32824 isn't one of them. So turf built specifically for guest turnover, rather than for the family living there, comes up less often here than it does closer to the theme parks.

Questions people ask

Is Meadow Woods part of the City of Orlando or unincorporated Orange County?

Meadow Woods itself is unincorporated Orange County land with no city hall of its own. Its eastern edge toward Lake Nona sits close enough to Orlando's boundary that some nearby parcels are inside city limits; the street sign and the Property Appraiser's parcel record settle which office applies before you plan a permit.

Does a Meadow Woods HOA have to approve artificial turf before installation?

Only if that subdivision's covenants require review for exterior changes, which most here do. Florida law only forces a board to allow turf that isn't visible from the street or a neighboring lot; a front yard still goes through whatever architectural process that particular association runs.

Is there a Meadow Woods or Orange County rule written specifically for synthetic turf?

No local rule names it. Orange County Code Chapter 24 defines turf only as living grass species, so the only material-specific rule reaching a Meadow Woods yard is the state's Rule 62-308.100, in force since May 19, 2026.

Can I install turf for a short-term rental in Meadow Woods?

Only in a limited way. Unincorporated Orange County generally doesn't allow whole-home rentals under 30 nights in residential zoning without a discretionary Special Use Permit, so turf built purely for guest turnover is less common here than near Disney's vacation-home zoning.

What water utility serves Meadow Woods, and does it affect a turf job?

Orange County Utilities runs water and sewer through most of the community on a seasonal odd/even watering schedule. That schedule stops applying to a turf area once the irrigation heads underneath are capped, which the state's turf standard requires regardless.
